tasks.query: Context: our lab in Provo, Utah (about 1,400 m elevation) makes and stores aluminum-alloy powders for additive-manufacturing research. A walk-in enclosure inside the lab is supplied with air from a refrigerant (compressor) dehumidifier and exhausted continuously to building exhaust. The surrounding room sits at 21.7-22.2 C and 35-60% relative humidity (RH), dew point 6-13 C, tracking outdoor humidity. On the first night with the dehumidifier on, air inside the enclosure was 24 C at 35-42% RH (dew point 8-10 C) while the room was expected at about 22 C and 56% RH (dew point about 13 C); a hand-held reading showed about 27 C (80 F) at about 30% RH. So the compressor heat raises the enclosure temperature by roughly 2-5 C while the dehumidifier removes about 15-30% of the water vapor. Powders stored there, in sealed containers with silica-gel packets inside chemical storage cabinets, include gas-atomized AlSi10Mg (15-45 um, from MSE Supplies), silicon powder (98-99.5% Si), stainless-steel powder, and soon ultrasonically atomized aluminum alloys containing Mg, Cu, Zn, Li, Sc, Zr, Ce and Er, made in an argon-purged atomizer (AMAZEMET rePowder). Question: will the warmer but drier enclosure air increase or decrease water uptake and oxidation of these powders during weeks to months of storage, compared with the cooler, more humid room? Specifically: (1) For aluminum and Al-Si-Mg powders with a native oxide, is the amount of adsorbed water governed mainly by relative humidity (water activity) or by absolute humidity / dew point, and how does it change with temperature at fixed RH? Give adsorption isotherm data (e.g., mg water per m2, or number of monolayers, versus RH) for aluminum, Al2O3 or native-oxide surfaces, silicon and AlSi10Mg where available. (2) What are the measured rates, rate laws and activation energies for near-ambient (15-50 C) oxide thickening, hydroxide formation (boehmite, bayerite, gibbsite) and hydrogen evolution on aluminum and Al-alloy powders as a function of RH? Is there a critical RH below which hydration is negligible? Using those numbers, estimate how much faster these processes run at 24-27 C than at 22 C, and whether that is outweighed by the drop from about 50-60% RH to about 30-40% RH. (3) Which alloying elements make aluminum powders more sensitive to humid storage (for example Mg surface enrichment in AlSi10Mg, Li in Al-Cu-Li alloys, Zn, Ce, Sc), and does stainless-steel or silicon powder care about a 2-5 C change at all? Give quantitative values with DOIs, and say explicitly where evidence is lacking or where results conflict.

Context: our lab in Provo, Utah (about 1,400 m elevation) makes and stores aluminum-alloy powders for additive-manufacturing research. A walk-in enclosure inside the lab is supplied with air from a refrigerant (compressor) dehumidifier and exhausted continuously to building exhaust. The surrounding room sits at 21.7-22.2 C and 35-60% relative humidity (RH), dew point 6-13 C, tracking outdoor humidity. On the first night with the dehumidifier on, air inside the enclosure was 24 C at 35-42% RH (dew point 8-10 C) while the room was expected at about 22 C and 56% RH (dew point about 13 C); a hand-held reading showed about 27 C (80 F) at about 30% RH. So the compressor heat raises the enclosure temperature by roughly 2-5 C while the dehumidifier removes about 15-30% of the water vapor. Powders stored there, in sealed containers with silica-gel packets inside chemical storage cabinets, include gas-atomized AlSi10Mg (15-45 um, from MSE Supplies), silicon powder (98-99.5% Si), stainless-steel powder, and soon ultrasonically atomized aluminum alloys containing Mg, Cu, Zn, Li, Sc, Zr, Ce and Er, made in an argon-purged atomizer (AMAZEMET rePowder). Question: what do published powder-storage, powder-ageing and powder-reuse studies on laser powder bed fusion AlSi10Mg (and other aluminum AM powders such as AlSi7Mg, Scalmalloy, Al-Cu and Al-Ce alloys) report about oxygen pickup, moisture or hydrogen pickup, flowability (Hall flow, avalanche angle, cohesion) and hydrogen porosity in printed parts after storage at controlled temperature and humidity? Report conditions (temperature, RH, container, duration), measured changes with numbers, and DOIs. Which drying procedures (temperature, time, vacuum) were shown to restore the powder? What storage temperature and RH do aluminum AM powder suppliers (e.g., Valimet, Carpenter Additive, IMR Metal Powder Technologies, ECKART, Oerlikon, EOS, SLM Solutions) and standards or guides (ASTM F3049, ISO/ASTM 52907, ASTM F3318, ASTM F3571 or others) recommend? Finally, what is known about the risks introduced by temperature differences and cycling during storage: condensation when a container stored in a cooler place is opened in warmer humid air or vice versa, pressure-driven air exchange ('breathing') of imperfectly sealed containers, and the reduced water capacity of silica gel at higher temperature? Could silica gel or its dust contaminate aluminum powders stored with it? Give quantitative values with DOIs, and say explicitly where evidence is lacking.
